summary:
Missouri's Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, enacted in 2023 as Senate Bill 49 and effective 28 August 2023, prohibits people under 18 from beginning gender-affirming hormones or puberty blockers, while allowing those already in treatment to continue, and bans all transition-related surgery for minors. The statute also bars MO HealthNet Medicaid from paying for gender-affirming care at any age, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, exposes violating providers to licence revocation and to patient lawsuits up to 15 years after treatment, and sunsets on 28 August 2027. Because the prohibition regulates Missouri providers rather than patients' residence, it governs care delivered in the state to any patient under 18.

The ban has been upheld at every stage documented in these sources. A judge denied a preliminary injunction on 29 August 2023. Trial ran in September 2024 in the 44th Judicial Circuit, where Judge Robert Craig Carter ruled the law constitutional on 25 November 2024, and on 13 January 2026 the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously upheld the prohibition on transition surgeries, cross-sex hormones and other care for minors, quoting the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court decision upholding Tennessee's comparable ban. The challenge was filed on 25 July 2023 in Cole County Circuit Court by Lambda Legal, the ACLU of Missouri and Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner for three families of transgender young people, medical providers, PFLAG National and GLMA; counsel announced an appeal after the November 2024 ruling. Lawmakers are moving to make the ban permanent rather than let it lapse, and a November 2026 ballot initiative seeks to prohibit such care indefinitely.

State identity documents carry a surgical requirement. Under Mo. Ann. Stat. § 193.215(9), changing the sex on a Missouri birth certificate requires a court order supported by certified proof on hospital letterhead, including the attending physician's licensing and contact information, stating that the petitioner's physical sex has been altered and the surgical changes are irreversible; the original certificate is struck through and the abstract marked amended. Two cases that had allowed an exception, 13AR-CV00157 heard 22 April 2013 and 13AR-CV00240 heard 20 May 2013, were invalidated and reversed in May 2022, leaving no workaround to the surgical requirement. Driver's licences followed a looser path: from 2016 to 2024 the Department of Revenue accepted Form 5532 for a gender-designation change after policy review, then reverted to requiring surgery documentation or a court order after an unspecified incident.

Missouri restricts transgender participation in school and college sport. Senate Bill 39, passed in May 2023 and signed 7 June 2023, requires public and private schools through college to limit sports participation to sex assigned at birth, and expires automatically on 28 August 2027.

State funding cuts off transition care inside Missouri prisons. Governor Mike Kehoe signed an appropriations measure effective 2 July 2026 stating that no funds shall be expended for any cross-sex hormones, or gender transition surgery undertaken for the purpose of any gender transition, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. Missouri is the seventh state in the country to bar gender-affirming care for inmates and the second in 2026 after Oklahoma; Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina have near-identical laws, while comparable Idaho and Georgia measures were blocked by federal courts.

The state operates a tipline for anonymous reporting of suspected violations of the care ban and general complaints about a "gender transition intervention".

Protection is partial. Missouri's hate crime statutes explicitly cover gender identity, defined as "having a self-image or identity not traditionally associated with one's gender", but the state's non-discrimination legislation does not address gender identity, leaving no statewide protection in employment, housing or public accommodations on that basis.
tangentialFactors:
State officials have previously used emergency powers against transgender adults as well as minors. In March and April 2023 the Missouri Attorney General issued emergency orders declaring youth gender care experimental and imposing social-media addiction screening, consent and dysphoria assessment requirements; a further order of April 2023, set to expire February 2024, declared adult care experimental and required three years of documented intense dysphoria, at least 15 psychiatric sessions over 18 months with at least 10 with the same therapist, full treatment of comorbidities, autism screening, 15-year adverse-effect tracking, annual dysphoria assessment, screening for social contagion, written consent every three months for three years and then every six months, and detailed compliance records. A judge temporarily blocked the adult order and the Attorney General withdrew it in May 2023; the youth orders were withdrawn on 16 May 2023. The orders are no longer in force, and they document the direction of state policy-making toward transgender adults.

Missouri's own recognition of same-sex marriages predated the national rule: the state recognised such marriages from other jurisdictions from November 2013 under Governor Jay Nixon's executive order on joint tax filing, upheld in Barrier v. Vasterling on 3 October 2014, licensing began after the rulings of 5 November 2014 and 7 November 2014, and Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015 was followed on 7 July 2015 by an executive order directing state agencies to comply. National recognition now governs; the Missouri history is context for how state institutions have behaved.

The care ban's 2027 sunset and the pending ballot initiative mean the legal position for a visitor planning treatment in Missouri is dated rather than settled, and the sources show the trend running toward permanence rather than expiry.
localsOnly:
Kansas City declared itself a sanctuary city for transgender individuals and rights in May 2023, and Columbia voted in February 2024 to include LGBT protections in its sanctuary ordinance.

Domestic partnership registries in Clayton, Columbia, Jackson County, Kansas City, Olivette, St. Louis and University City grant certain benefits within their borders to both opposite- and same-sex couples.

Missouri has no statute limiting adoption on the basis of LGBT status under Mo. Ann. Stat. § 453.010, with no explicit prohibition on same-sex or second-parent adoption as of 2009. State non-discrimination law does not cover sexual orientation either: only a 2010 executive order protects government employees, and a Senate-passed bill of 2013 that passed 19-11 died when the House adjourned without considering it.

Residents and state prisoners bear the direct weight of the SAFE Act funding and coverage bars, including the July 2026 appropriations restriction on hormones and surgery for inmates already receiving care.
outOfScopeNotes:
These sources document no Missouri statute or regulation restricting transgender people's use of restrooms, changing rooms or other sex-segregated facilities. Whether such a restriction exists at state level is unresolved here; the parent record's count of states with facility bans does not name Missouri.

No Missouri-specific figures on violence or hate crimes against transgender people appear in the inventory. The hate crime statute's coverage of gender identity is documented, but enforcement, case counts and outcomes are not.

The "unspecified incident" that prompted the Department of Revenue to reverse its licence gender-marker policy between 2016 and 2024 is not identified in any source.

Whether the SAFE Act's 28 August 2027 sunset will stand, be repealed early or be overtaken by the November 2026 ballot initiative is unresolved; legislative proposals to make the ban permanent are described as pending.

The appeal announced after the 25 November 2024 ruling is not separately documented beyond the Missouri Supreme Court's 13 January 2026 affirmance, and the sources do not say whether further review was sought.

Implementation of the 2 July 2026 prison funding bar is not sourced beyond the report that no taper plan exists for inmates already receiving care; how existing prescriptions are handled in practice is not documented.

Entry screening, federal passport and visa rules, and federal custody policy are carried by the parent record and are not addressed for Missouri in these sources.
